approachQuestion.prompt: Choose a subset of n indivisible tools to fit capacity W and maximize total utility. Tool i has positive integer weight w[i] and non-negative integer utility u[i]. Each tool can be chosen at most once; unused capacity is allowed. Return only maximum utility. Examples: w=[2,3,4], u=[4,5,8], W=5 → 9; w=[4], u=[7], W=3 → 0. Which approach is most suitable?
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200; 1 ≤ W ≤ 10000; 1 ≤ w[i] ≤ 10000; 0 ≤ u[i] ≤ 1000000. Input arrays are read-only; utility fits signed 64-bit.

options.text: Initialize best[0..W] to zero for at-most capacities. For each tool, scan capacities from W downward to its weight, setting best[c]=max(best[c],best[c−w]+u). Return best[W].
options.feedback: The previous-item values remain intact at smaller capacities during a descending scan. Zero initialization allows the empty subset and any unused capacity.

options.text: Keep best utility for every item prefix and capacity in a full table, considering skip or take from the preceding row.
options.feedback: This computes the correct result on the whole domain, but retains old states that future transitions never read. Removing those states preserves correctness and reduces auxiliary storage.

options.text: For each tool update capacities upward using the same one-array formula.
options.feedback: For one tool of weight 2 and utility 3 with W=4, this returns 6 by using the same tool twice; the legal answer is 3.

options.text: Select tools by descending utility per weight, taking each that fits.
options.feedback: With weights [3,2,2], utilities [5,3,3], W=4, this takes weight 3 for utility 5, missing the two weight-2 tools worth 6.

feedback.reason: Model an at-most budget correctly and distinguish a 0/1 utility recurrence from an unbounded one.
details: Allocate W+1 zeroed utility entries. For each of n tools update all fitting capacities downward, without early exits, and return best[W].

Descending capacities ensure a tool contributes at most once. The include candidate uses the pre-tool state at capacity minus its weight. Ascending updates would solve a reusable-tool problem instead.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Allocate W+1 zeroed utility entries. For each of n tools update all fitting capacities downward, without early exits, and return best[W]. Analyze this fixed implementation. N=n; n,W vary independently. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Array indexing and word arithmetic take constant time. No hashing, amortized containers, recursion, slicing, or input copying is used. Count all allocated work arrays and temporaries; exclude the read-only input and scalar output.
Include initialization; treat the stated dimensions as variable parameters within their bounds. Use a word per stored counter or flag, not a packed bitset.

feedback.reason: Each tool can update W capacities in one retained utility array.
details: At worst each item scans nearly W capacities. Initialization costs W, dominated because n is positive. The only growing allocation is W+1 utility entries.
“O(n+W) time, O(W) auxiliary space”: Each tool can scan nearly W capacities, so the repeated work multiplies these dimensions.
“O(nW) time, O(nW) auxiliary space”: One capacity row is retained, not one row for each tool.
“O(nW) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Updating downward avoids a second row but does not eliminate the W+1 utility entries.
